payload.rationale: The contract resolves YES only if the headline CPI (single-decimal, presumably seasonally adjusted month-over-month) prints 0.5% or higher for October 2026. Historically, outside the 2021–2022 inflation surge, monthly prints of 0.5%+ are uncommon: in 2023–2025 the large majority of prints fell between 0.0% and 0.4%, with 0.5%+ occurring only a few times per year at most, typically driven by energy spikes. Assuming underlying inflation in late 2026 runs roughly 2.5–3.5% annualized (a monthly mean near 0.25%) with a typical month-to-month standard deviation around 0.15 percentage points, the chance of a print at or above 0.45% (rounding to 0.5%) is roughly 8–12%. Fat tails from energy/shelter shocks or tariff pass-through argue for the upper part of that range; the absence of any supplied evidence about current conditions in September 2026 means I rely mainly on base rates. Too high: if inflation has decelerated toward 2% by fall 2026, or energy prices are soft, a 0.5% print would be quite unlikely (perhaps 5%). Too low: if tariffs, energy, or a reaccelerating economy have pushed monthly core prints toward 0.3–0.4%, or a sharp gasoline spike hits in October, the probability could be 20%+. Also note potential release-timing complications (e.g., government shutdown) which do not change the event but add settlement uncertainty.
limitations: No current research or data supplied; estimate is based on historical base rates and general background knowledge only.
Unknown macro conditions (energy prices, tariff pass-through, labor market) as of September–October 2026.
Assumes contract references seasonally adjusted headline CPI-U month-over-month change as published by BLS.
